passage: Tanvir's Abba bought him a small packet of cream biscuits from the kirana shop below their Bengaluru apartment. There were only four inside. Chandrika from the third floor had none. She looked at the packet, then at her shoes. Tanvir ate one slowly, licking out the cream. It was his favourite kind. He looked at the three left, then at Chandrika. He held one out, pulled it back a little, then held it out again. "One for you," he said. "And the last one we break." He snapped it and gave her the bigger half by mistake. He frowned, but let her keep it.

qa.q: How many biscuits were in the packet?
qa.a: There were only four biscuits inside.

qa.q: What does Tanvir pulling the biscuit back and then holding it out again show?
qa.a: He felt torn between keeping his favourite biscuits and sharing with Chandrika, and his kindness won.

qa.q: How could Abba respond to what Tanvir did?
qa.a: He could tell Tanvir he noticed that sharing a favourite treat was hard and that he did it anyway, so Tanvir values the choice.

qa.q: How might Chandrika feel standing there without any biscuits?
qa.a: She probably felt left out and shy, so being offered one likely felt warm and surprising.

grounding: It shows a child sharing a small, favourite treat even though it costs him something he wanted.

passage:
"I need pink for the flower," said Irawati.
Pema hugged the pink crayon. "I need it for my princess."
"But you've had it for ages."
"It's the only pink. And it's my favourite."
Mama called from the kitchen, "What's the fight, girls?"
"No fight," Pema called back. She looked at the crayon, then at Irawati's empty flower. "You can do your flower. Then give it back, okay?"
"Okay. I'll be quick."
"Not too quick. Colour it nicely." Pema handed it over and started on her princess's hair in yellow instead.

qa.q: What colour did Pema use for her princess's hair instead?
qa.a: She used yellow.

qa.q: What does Pema hugging the crayon suggest she felt about sharing it?
qa.a: She hugged it, said it was her favourite and the only pink, and made Irawati promise to give it back.

qa.q: What could Mama say if she walks in now?
qa.a: She might notice aloud that Pema gave up her favourite crayon while she still wanted it, without making a big fuss.

qa.q: How might Irawati feel when Pema tells her to colour it nicely?
qa.a: She may feel trusted and relieved, and more willing to share with Pema next time. 😊

grounding: It shows a young child giving up the only pink crayon to her sister even though she wanted it herself.

passage: Note by Nazia, preschool teacher. At playtime Himani had the only swing that works, the one she waits for all morning. A new girl stood near the pole, holding the chain of the broken swing. Himani swung three times, slowed, and swung again. Then she dragged her feet and stopped. "You can have five swings," she told the new girl, and counted them aloud for her, frowning a little on the last two. Afterwards she got her turn back. I told her I had noticed. Tomorrow I will ask for the other swing to be fixed. 😊

qa.q: How many swings did Himani offer the new girl?
qa.a: She offered her five swings.

qa.q: What does Himani frowning on the last two counts suggest?
qa.a: She was eager to get her turn back and found giving up the swing hard, even while choosing to share it.

qa.q: Why is Nazia's plan to fix the other swing useful?
qa.a: With two working swings, children won't have to give up so much, so sharing can feel lighter and fairer.

qa.q: What was it like for the new girl standing by the broken swing?
qa.a: She was probably unsure and left out, so Himani's offer made her feel welcome.

grounding: It shows a child sharing the only working swing with a newcomer despite wanting it herself.

passage: Under the mango tree near the village pond, Preeti had two ripe guavas from her Nani's tree. She had been saving them all afternoon. Yamini came and sat beside her, looking. Preeti held both guavas close to her chest and bit her lip. Then she sighed and held one out. 'You take this. It's the smaller one.' She paused. 'No, take the big one.' They ate side by side, slurping.

qa.q: Where did Preeti's guavas come from?
qa.a: They came from her Nani's tree.

qa.q: What does Preeti biting her lip and holding the guavas close suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she really wanted to keep both and felt torn about giving one away.

qa.q: How could Nani encourage Preeti's sharing without forcing it?
qa.a: She could notice it later and say it was kind, letting Preeti feel the good of sharing on her own.

qa.q: What might Yamini feel when Preeti hands her the big guava?
qa.a: She would likely feel surprised and happy, and closer to Preeti. 😊

grounding: Illustrates a young child sharing a limited treat despite wanting it herself, in a village.

passage: In their Vancouver kitchen, only one cookie was left in the tin. Chen grabbed it first. His sister Leila's face fell. Chen looked at the cookie, then at her. He held it up and turned it round. 'I really wanted this,' he said slowly. Then he snapped it in half. One half was bigger. He held both out. 'You pick.' Leila took the smaller piece and smiled.

qa.q: How many cookies were left in the tin?
qa.a: Only one cookie was left.

qa.q: How was Chen feeling when he said 'I really wanted this' before breaking the cookie?
qa.a: He felt torn between wanting the cookie for himself and wanting to share with Leila, which made the choice hard.

qa.q: Which part of Chen's choice was especially fair?
qa.a: Letting Leila pick her half gave her a real choice, which is a kind and fair way to split a treat.

qa.q: How might Leila see her brother after this?
qa.a: She may feel he cares about her, since he gave up something he wanted.

grounding: Shows a young child sharing a limited treat even though he wanted it for himself, in Canada.

passage: At the kindergarten birthday party, the teacher gave out chocolates, but there was one short. Dilnaz, the last in line, got nothing. Anirban, five, had just unwrapped his. He looked at the chocolate, then at Dilnaz, then back. He loved chocolate. Slowly, he broke it in half and held out the bigger piece. "Here." Dilnaz beamed. Anirban ate his half very, very slowly.

qa.q: Who got no chocolate?
qa.a: Dilnaz, the last in line.

qa.q: Why did Anirban look back and forth before breaking his chocolate?
qa.a: He was torn between wanting all of it and feeling bad for Dilnaz.

qa.q: How could the teacher show Anirban his sharing mattered?
qa.a: Thank him quietly and tell him it was kind, especially as he loves chocolate.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz feel when Anirban shares?
qa.a: Happy and included, instead of left out at the party.

grounding: Shows a young child sharing a treat he loves when there is not enough to go round.

passage: I'm Kalyani, Kavitha's big sister. On Sankranti, Kavitha, who is five, got her first kite. She was so happy she slept with it. The next day the neighbour's boy was crying because his kite had torn. Kavitha held her kite behind her back. Then she walked over and said, "We can fly mine. You hold the string first." I was surprised; she never shares new things. I'm not sure how she felt, but she kept checking the kite was okay.

qa.q: When did Kavitha get her first kite?
qa.a: On Sankranti.

qa.q: What might Kavitha have felt when she held her kite behind her back?
qa.a: She was probably torn, wanting to keep her new kite safe but feeling sorry for the crying boy.

qa.q: How could Kalyani encourage Kavitha's sharing?
qa.a: Tell her it was kind and help them take turns so the kite stays safe.

qa.q: How does Kalyani see Kavitha's choice?
qa.a: Kalyani is surprised, since Kavitha usually doesn't share new things, but only guesses at the feeling.

grounding: Shows a young child sharing a new, precious kite with an upset neighbour, seen by an older sister.

passage: Monday: Darshan, five, got the only ripe mango from Dada Manoj's tree and ate it all, even when his little cousin cried. Thursday: another mango ripened. Darshan hugged it, then gave his cousin one slice, frowning. Dada Manoj said nothing, only smiled. The next Sunday: there was just one mango again. Darshan cut it himself with Dada's help and gave his cousin the first piece. "You first," he said.

qa.q: Whose tree did the mango come from?
qa.a: Dada Manoj's tree.

qa.q: What does Darshan frowning as he gave the slice suggest?
qa.a: He was reluctant and a little sad to give up part of the mango, but did it anyway.

qa.q: What helped Darshan move towards sharing?
qa.a: Dada Manoj letting him choose without scolding, so the sharing came from Darshan himself.

qa.q: How might the cousin feel on Sunday?
qa.a: Surprised and happy to get the first piece this time.

grounding: Shows a young child moving over a week from keeping a treat to sharing it first.

passage: The bus was stuck in traffic outside Pune for over an hour. Simran had one small chocolate left, the one she'd saved all day. Her cousin Chaitanya, three, had cried himself hoarse and was now kicking the seat. "Hungry," he whimpered. Simran looked at the chocolate. She really wanted all of it. She broke it, made the two halves nearly equal, then gave him the slightly bigger one. Chaitanya went quiet, chocolate on his chin. Simran nibbled her half very slowly to make it last.

qa.q: How long was the bus stuck in traffic?
qa.a: For over an hour.

qa.q: What was Simran feeling when she looked at the chocolate?
qa.a: She was torn; she really wanted it all but could see how hungry and upset Chaitanya was.

qa.q: What could an adult on the bus say to Simran afterwards?
qa.a: They could thank her warmly for sharing the chocolate she had saved, noticing that it was hard to give up.

qa.q: How was Chaitanya affected by Simran's choice?
qa.a: The hungry little boy calmed down and stopped crying once he had the chocolate.

grounding: A five-year-old shares her only chocolate with a crying cousin on a delayed bus despite wanting it herself.

passage: Holi morning in the Andheri colony. Pallavi had a brand-new water pistol, green and shiny. Ira from the second floor had nothing but her hands, and she stood near the gate watching the other kids splash. Pallavi squirted one more stream at the wall. Then she walked over and held the pistol out. "Your turn. Five squirts, then mine." Ira's face lit up. Pallavi counted each squirt out loud, fists clenched, then took it back and handed it again after her own five.

qa.q: What colour was Pallavi's water pistol?
qa.a: Green and shiny.

qa.q: What was Pallavi feeling while Ira had her turn?
qa.a: She felt reluctant and a little anxious about her new toy, clenching her fists and counting every squirt out loud.

qa.q: What could a parent watching from the balcony say to Pallavi?
qa.a: They could tell her it was kind to share her new toy, and that taking turns looked like fun for both girls.

qa.q: What was Holi morning like for Ira before and after Pallavi came over?
qa.a: At first Ira felt left out, watching from the gate; then her face lit up as she joined the play.

grounding: A child shares her new water pistol with a girl who has none during Holi, though she wants to keep using it.

passage:
On Sankranti evening, Abhinav held the last sesame chikki.
"Bhaiya, give!" said Jagdish, reaching.
"It's mine. I saved it."
"I didn't get one." Jagdish's lip shook.
Dadaji looked up from the kite string. "Hmm. What will you do?"
Abhinav held the chikki tighter. "I want it."
"I know."
Abhinav snapped it in two. "Here. But mine's the bigger one."
Jagdish bit his half. "Crunchy!"
Abhinav chewed and grinned. "Tomorrow you share your kite."
"Deal!"

qa.q: What was Dadaji doing when he looked up?
qa.a: He was working on the kite string.

qa.q: What was Abhinav feeling when he said, "I want it"?
qa.a: He felt possessive and reluctant; he had saved the chikki and wanted it for himself.

qa.q: What worked about Dadaji's question "What will you do?"
qa.a: It let Abhinav make the choice himself, so the sharing came from him rather than an order.

qa.q: How did Jagdish feel when Abhinav refused at first, and then when he got his half?
qa.a: Jagdish looked close to tears at first, then seemed happy with the crunchy half.

grounding: A young boy splits his last chikki with a younger child though he wanted it, after a grandfather asks what he'll do.

passage:
Kindergarten note, Christmas party.

Each child got one piece of plum cake. Vandana ate half of hers. Then she saw that Rinku's had fallen on the floor.

She looked at her half for a long time. Then she broke it again and gave Rinku the bigger bit. "You have this."

She told me later, "I wanted it. But Rinku didn't have any." — Manoj

qa.q: What happened to Rinku's cake?
qa.a: Rinku's had fallen on the floor.

qa.q: How did Vandana feel about giving away her cake?
qa.a: Vandana felt torn, because she wanted it but felt sorry that Rinku had none.

qa.q: How can Manoj encourage Vandana's sharing?
qa.a: He can notice and praise her kindness, especially since she gave up something she wanted.

qa.q: How might Rinku feel when Vandana gave the cake?
qa.a: Rinku would likely feel happy and grateful.

grounding: A kindergarten note records a child sharing her Christmas cake even though she wanted it herself.

passage:
At the Lohri bonfire in the village near Jalandhar, Gurpreet, five, had a fistful of rewri. Keerthana, visiting from Chennai, had none.

Gurpreet looked at his sweets, then at her. He put one in his mouth. Then he held out his fist. "Take two."

Keerthana took two. Gurpreet looked at the rest and gave her one more. "Three. Now we both have three."

qa.q: How many rewri did Keerthana end up with?
qa.a: She ended up with three.

qa.q: How did Gurpreet feel about sharing?
qa.a: Gurpreet seemed a bit reluctant at first, but then generous and fair, wanting them both to have the same.

qa.q: How could adults encourage Gurpreet's sharing?
qa.a: They could praise him for sharing fairly with a guest.

qa.q: How might Keerthana feel being given rewri?
qa.a: Keerthana would likely feel welcomed and happy.

grounding: At a Lohri bonfire, a child shares his sweets with a visiting child even though he wants them.

passage:
On Halloween night in Dublin, Liam and Santiago went trick-or-treating together. At the last house, Santiago's bag split, and his sweets rolled into a drain.

Santiago cried.

Liam looked into his own bag. He had ten sweets. He had been planning to eat them all.

He counted out five and put them in Santiago's hands. "Half each."

Santiago wiped his eyes. "Thanks, Liam."

qa.q: How many sweets did Liam give Santiago?
qa.a: He counted out five.

qa.q: How did Liam feel about giving away half his sweets?
qa.a: Liam felt a little reluctant, since he had planned to eat them all, but he cared that Santiago was sad.

qa.q: How could an adult support Liam's sharing?
qa.a: Praise him for giving up something he wanted to help his friend.

qa.q: How might Santiago feel when Liam shared?
qa.a: Santiago would likely feel comforted and grateful.

grounding: On Halloween, a child shares half his sweets with a friend who lost his.

passage: On the last day before the Christmas break, the kindergarten in Shillong had a party. Each child got one star cookie. Neelam had been in the washroom and came back to an empty plate. Her lip trembled. Gargi looked at her own cookie, the last iced star she'd been saving. She broke it in half, slowly, and held out the bigger piece. "You can have this one." Then she looked at her small half and sighed. Teacher Iba smiled. "That was generous, Gargi."

qa.q: What kind of cookie did each child get?
qa.a: Each child got one star cookie.

qa.q: Why did Gargi sigh at her small half?
qa.a: She felt a little sorry to lose part of her treat, even though she chose to share; she felt both kind and disappointed.

qa.q: How could Teacher Iba make sure no child misses out next time?
qa.a: She could keep treats aside for anyone out of the room, while still noticing kind acts like Gargi's.

qa.q: What is it like for Neelam to receive the bigger piece?
qa.a: Neelam probably feels relieved and grateful, and cared for by Gargi. 😊

grounding: Shows a young child sharing a scarce party treat even though it costs her some of her own pleasure.
